question: A 3-year-old is brought in after witnessed peanut aspiration. He is now comfortable, oxygen saturations are 97%, and the inspiratory CXR appears normal. What is the correct management?

answers.text: Discharge home and advise parents to return if symptoms worsen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discharge is unsafe when there is a witnessed aspiration event. Radiolucent foreign bodies (peanuts) appear normal on CXR; the object is still in the airway until proven otherwise.

answers.text: Observe for 24 hours with serial CXRs; refer for bronchoscopy only if a CXR abnormality develops

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serial CXRs cannot detect a radiolucent peanut. The diagnosis is clinical + history; waiting for CXR changes risks complete obstruction or delayed presentation.

answers.text: Proceed to rigid bronchoscopy for definitive diagnosis and extraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Witnessed aspiration of a radiolucent object (peanut) is a definitive indication for rigid bronchoscopy regardless of CXR findings. Bronchoscopy is simultaneously diagnostic and therapeutic.

answers.text: Order a CT chest with HRCT protocol to localise the peanut before bronchoscopy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is not routinely required before bronchoscopy in a witnessed aspiration. It adds radiation dose and delays definitive treatment. CT is reserved for equivocal presentations or complications.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: bronchoscopy is indicated on the strength of the history, not contingent on an abnormal CXR. A radiolucent peanut will never appear on a plain film.
Correct. Witnessed aspiration → bronchoscopy, full stop. A normal CXR does not change the indication.
